references.text: Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at the well and asks her for water – a parallel to Jesus' meeting with the Samaritan woman at the well. Both scenes involve an encounter at a well where water is requested, and both lead to a significant revelation ([ref:Gen 24:13-17|Genesis 24:13-17]).

Jacob meets Rachel at the well – another example of the classic biblical motif of a life-changing encounter at a well. Jesus meets the Samaritan woman in a similar way ([ref:Gen 29:9-10|Genesis 29:9-10]).
Moses meets Zipporah at the well in Midian. The 'well encounter' motif in the Old Testament forms the background for Jesus' meeting with the woman at Jacob's well ([ref:Exod 2:15-17|Exodus 2:15-17]).

Elijah asks the widow of Zarephath for water to drink – a prophet asking a foreign woman for water, just as Jesus asks the Samaritan woman. Both cases break cultural barriers ([ref:1 Kgs 17:10-11|1 Kings 17:10-11]).

The woman's immediate reaction to Jesus' request reveals the cultural and ethnic tension between Jews and Samaritans, explaining the surprising nature of Jesus asking her for water ([ref:John 4:9|John 4:9]).

Jesus' request for physical water in verse 7 becomes the starting point for his revelation about living water – the earthly need points to the spiritual gift he offers ([ref:John 4:10-14|John 4:10-14]).

Jesus' words 'I am thirsty' on the cross form a deep theological parallel to his request for water here. He who offers living water experiences the deepest thirst himself ([ref:John 19:28|John 19:28]).

"With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation" – the prophecy about the waters of salvation forms the background for Jesus' offer of living water, which begins with his simple request to be given a drink ([ref:Isa 12:3|Isaiah 12:3]).

The water motif in Isaiah's invitation – "All you who are thirsty, come to the water" – resonates with Jesus' conversation that starts from physical thirst and leads to spiritual water ([ref:Isa 55:1|Isaiah 55:1]).

The Lord accuses his people of having forsaken him, 'the fountain of living waters,' and hewn out cisterns that cannot hold water. This prophecy adds depth to Jesus' offer of living water at Jacob's well ([ref:Jer 2:13|Jeremiah 2:13]).
